claims.text: As-received, pre-exposure Q235 steel has a native oxide layer.
The native oxide scale on Q235 steel is porous, non-adherent Fe2O3.
Controlled annealing transforms the native Fe2O3 scale into a denser and more adherent Fe3O4 layer.
Annealing changes the defect density and phase composition of the pre-existing oxide layer.
An optimal annealing condition is expected near 800 °C for an appropriate fixed duration.
The Fe3O4 layer formed under optimal annealing limits the diffusion of oxygen and salt ions.
Limiting oxygen and salt-ion diffusion improves protection during high-temperature salt exposure.
Insufficient annealing leaves the oxide scale porous and diminishes corrosion resistance.
Excessive annealing produces an overly thick scale that is prone to cracking during thermal cycling.
Cracking of the excessively thick oxide scale diminishes corrosion resistance.
Q235 specimens annealed at 700, 800, and 900 °C can be compared with unannealed controls to isolate the effect of annealing.

Optimally annealed Q235 steel, particularly near 800 °C, will exhibit statistically significant reductions in mass change and corrosion rate during high-temperature salt exposure relative to unannealed or over-annealed specimens.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply when intrinsic oxide-formation and phase-transformation kinetics dominate corrosion behavior.
The proposed mechanism may not apply when additional alloying or drastically different atmospheres independently alter oxidation.
Small changes in annealing temperature or time may produce inconclusive effects because of overlapping thermal phenomena.
Transformations occurring during prolonged high-temperature exposure may obscure the influence of the initially annealed oxide scale.
